blogs.title: The 0.3 mg Trap: Why 'Adult' Autoinjectors May Be Underdosing
blogs.description: We analyze the discrepancy between standard 0.3 mg epinephrine auto-injectors and guidelines recommending 0.5 mg for adults over 50 kg. Drawing from recent retrospective data and the case presented, we discuss how underdosing can lead to recurrent anaphylactic shock and the need for dose adjustment in the ED.

blogs.title: Steroids Save Who? Re-evaluating the Role of Corticosteroids in Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: A critical look at the practice of administering corticosteroids during anaphylaxis. We contrast the historical assumption that they prevent biphasic reactions with recent systematic reviews suggesting no proven benefit and potential harm, urging clinicians to align protocols with current evidence.

blogs.title: Tryptase Timing: Crucial Lessons from Missed Peaks
blogs.description: This post explores the strict timing requirements for serum tryptase sampling in anaphylaxis (peak during symptoms, baseline 24 hours post-recovery). We examine how missing these windows hinders the diagnosis of underlying conditions and complicates management of recurrent cases.

blogs.title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Recognizing Systemic Mastocytosis in Recurrent Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: We highlight the clinical clues that should trigger suspicion for systemic mastocytosis rather than common drug allergy. Key differentiators discussed include hepatomegaly, history of psychiatric symptoms, and persistent elevated tryptase levels despite resolution.

blogs.title: Don't Just Wait: Continuous Infusion vs. Expectant Observation in Multiphasic Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Facing a patient with recurrent shock, do you treat prophylactically or reactively? We discuss the lack of consensus on continuous epinephrine infusions versus expectant management in multiphasic courses, outlining the risks and benefits of each approach in the ICU.

blogs.title: Four Hours Isn't Enough: Re-thinking Observation Durations for Biphasic Reactions
blogs.description: Standard guidelines suggest a 4-6 hour observation period after initial resolution. In multiphasic cases, this threshold may be dangerous. We evaluate the evidence suggesting recurrence can occur up to 78 hours later and propose risk-stratified decision-making for discharge monitoring.
